children: By Katherine Clarke

In March 2023, cosmetics billionaire William P. Lauder paid $155 million for the longtime oceanfront estate of the late radio host Rush Limbaugh, setting a then-record for Florida's Palm Beach. The roughly 24,000-square-foot main house, built in the early 1990s, had a grand salon modeled after Versailles and a library styled after one at the Biltmore Estate in Asheville, N.C., complete with carved cherubs on the ceiling.
By July, Lauder had demolished it.

The destruction of the Limbaugh house is one of the most extreme examples of a trend playing out in wealthy enclaves across the country: the $100 million-plus teardown. The house, once the central reason for making a big-ticket property purchase, has become almost beside the point as buyers compete for well-positioned land — a stretch of oceanfront or mountaintop that can't be replicated, unlike the house sitting on it.

The wealthy have long knocked down older houses, or those in need of substantial renovation, to start fresh. But large, relatively new houses in good repair are now being purchased for eye-popping price tags, then razed to make way for homes more in keeping with today's styles. The trend, with Palm Beach at its epicenter, is drawing criticism for its potential impact on the environment.

"It would seem that these homes are beautiful and livable, with higher-end appliances, cabinetry, countertops, those types of things," said Robert Burrage, a South Florida-based contractor who has worked on multiple uber-luxury homes. "But not to the guy who has $100 million and wants what he wants the way he wants it."
Demolition derby

Palm Beach has become a hotbed for eight and nine-figure teardowns, thanks to its ultrahigh net worth population and limited inventory of oceanfront land. "It's logical that this would be an increasing phenomenon," said real-estate appraiser Jonathan Miller. "As the land gets more expensive, the cost to replace the house drops as a percentage."

Lauder, for example, previously demolished two houses on about 3 oceanfront acres in a different section of Palm Beach. He had planned to build a house for himself there before finding the Limbaugh site, according to people familiar with the situation. Instead, he sold the vacant land for close to $200 million in 2025 to a buyer with links to software giant Microsoft. Lauder declined to comment.
One of the houses Lauder demolished was only six years old, in what real-estate agents now call "a double teardown": a house razed and rebuilt twice in just a handful of years.

In the nearby town of Manalapan, WeatherTech founder David MacNeil has also developed a reputation for tearing down massive homes. He recently paid $55.5 million for a partially completed mansion next door to an oceanfront lot he owned. Then, he tore down the home and sold the assemblage for $105 million earlier this year, according to people familiar with that deal.

MacNeil also demolished a circa-2004, roughly 9,000-square-foot Manalapan home after buying it for $36 million in July. He plans to replace the house, which is directly adjacent to his main home, with a fitness center and green space.

"You might go, 'Well, you tore a perfectly good house down.' Well, no, it wasn't a perfectly good house," said MacNeil. "It was dated. It was suffering from deferred maintenance. It probably needed a $10 million restoration to get it up to a modern standard, and we didn't go for that."

As a rule, he said, if land adjacent to his becomes available and he can afford it, he buys it. "If I didn't buy that house, somebody else would, and then I would have to deal with their construction, their design, their nonsense," he said.

As demand has spiked, real-estate agents have leaned in to marketing existing mansions as teardowns, using AI to generate images of what the empty site would look like. Many don't love the word "teardown," preferring terms like "adaptive reuse" to avoid offending their seller clients.

Agent Gary Pohrer of Serhant recently listed the circa-1980s home of late real-estate developer Murray Goodman and his wife, Joanie Goodman, for $185 million. The home is in good condition, but is likely to be demolished so a buyer can build something more modern, local agents said.

Billionaire tech titan Larry Ellison also recently relisted his circa-1990s home in North Palm Beach for $165 million. While the Tuscan-style home itself is in good condition, listing agents James Kenny and Paul Kaneb of K2 Realty said they are marketing it as a potential redevelopment because many ultrawealthy buyers would likely build a home to their own tastes.
While some sellers find it hard to accept that their once-beloved homes will be turned to rubble, others are resigned.
Kathryn Adams Limbaugh, Rush Limbaugh's widow, said she met Lauder before the sale closed and liked him, though she deliberately avoided learning his plans for the house.
She said she "certainly cannot fault" Lauder for how he and his family plan to use the property. "It was their property to do as they wished."
Environmental consequences?

Tearing down a mansion — particularly to replace it with a larger one — can have meaningful environmental consequences, according to William Paddock of the environmental-consulting firm WAP Sustainability. His company estimates that replacing a 10,000-square-foot house with a 30,000-square-foot one results in a similar carbon footprint to powering approximately 250 average U.S. homes for a year.
"When things are torn down unnecessarily and put into landfills, that's really difficult," said Danielle Del Sol of the Preservation Foundation of Palm Beach.

Burrage, however, said that it's a misconception that teardown homes are entirely scraped into landfills. Burrage estimated that when his firm tears down a home, only about 25% of the materials go into landfills. The firm donates appliances and cabinetry, and sorts materials like concrete and metal that can be used for other purposes.
The teardown trend is playing out across the country in markets where inventory of buildable land is constrained. And it isn't just billionaires and $100 million homes.

Redfin's economists say they see teardown-related language, such as "rebuild," and "land value," in a significant percentage of home listings. In Houston's Bunker Hill Village, where midcentury homes are frequently replaced with more modern ones, more than 15 percent of listings include teardown terms, according to Redfin. Pimmit Hills, V.A., a classic postwar suburban neighborhood in Fairfax County that has become a hot spot for home teardowns, saw 6.67%.

Near Destin, retired retail executives Jamie Dulick and Kristin Scott paid $3.7 million for a beachfront teardown in 2020 and spent five years replacing it with a new, modern home. They said they took on the project because it was the only available oceanfront lot in the enclave they wanted to be in.

"I had people calling me up within a couple of months of us closing on it, and just offering me ridiculous amounts of money above what we had paid," Dulick said. Ultimately, the couple put the completed house on the market for $18.9 million and are looking for another teardown.

In Miami, agent Dina Goldentayer of Douglas Elliman said many of her clients are no longer impressed by the style of homes built less than a decade ago, which is making double teardowns more common. When they can't find what they want, they quickly pivot to looking at properties that can be replaced.

Ending up with the right home often trumps energy efficiency and wastefulness, Goldentayer said. "The bottom line," she said, "is these people are billionaires and they don't want to have ugly kitchens and baths."
